title: Acute Hypoxaemic Respiratory Failure: Oxygen, Non-Invasive Ventilation and ICU Referral
specialty: Respiratory Medicine / Critical Care / Emergency Medicine

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure in the emergency department (ED) or on a ward: target-based oxygen prescribing, choice between conventional oxygen, high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) and non-invasive ventilation (NIV), recognition of hypercapnia, and timely referral to the intensive care unit (ICU) for invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV). Uses the British Thoracic Society (BTS) 2017 oxygen guideline summary, an NHS Borders policy adapted from the BTS guideline, the European Respiratory Society (ERS) 2022 high-flow guideline and the BTS/Intensive Care Society 2016 hypercapnic respiratory failure guideline. Disease-specific treatment (pneumonia, heart failure, pulmonary embolism) is in separate topics.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-21.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi guideline on acute respiratory failure or oxygen prescribing was found.

The full BTS 2017 oxygen guideline was not opened; the hospital summary (Web Appendix 3) and an NHS Borders policy derived from the earlier BTS guideline are used. The NHS Borders policy (2013) was past its review date.

ERS 2022 gives no formal definition or blood-gas threshold for acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure and no high-flow settings for hypoxaemic patients; the flow range 35 to 60 L/min it reports is from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) studies.
No ERS or BTS criterion for when to intubate a hypoxaemic patient was found; the decision is clinical and made with the ICU team.
Typical adult arterial blood gas ranges are not from these guidelines.

pathophysiology.summary: Oxygen is given to prevent cellular hypoxia from hypoxaemia and protect vital organs (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 6.0). Common causes of acute hypoxaemia are pneumonia, shock, asthma, heart failure and pulmonary embolism (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 6.0). In patients with chronic carbon dioxide retention (COPD, neuromuscular disease, morbid obesity, chest wall disease), excess oxygen can raise carbon dioxide and cause respiratory acidosis (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 8.1). Hypercapnic failure is pump failure: alveolar ventilation is too low to keep carbon dioxide normal; co-existing hypoxaemia is usually mild (BTS/ICS 2016, Definition of acute hypercapnic respiratory failure). Prolonging non-invasive support in a patient who is failing can delay intubation and may worsen mortality (ERS 2022, Results: HFNC for hypoxaemic acute respiratory failure).

symptoms: Distress or agitation during ventilatory support may need closely monitored sedation (BTS/ICS 2016, Recommendations 7 and 9).
physicalSigns: Oxygen saturation below 90% with or without oxygen (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.4).
Respiratory rate below 8 or above 25 breaths per minute (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.4).
Noisy or laboured breathing (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.4).
Peripheral cyanosis (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.4).
redFlags: Peri-arrest or critically ill: 15 L/min oxygen via reservoir mask while awaiting immediate review (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.5).
Any sudden fall in saturation: clinical review and, in most cases, blood gases (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.4).
pH below 7.35 with carbon dioxide above 6.5 kPa: hypercapnic failure needing ventilatory support (BTS/ICS 2016, Recommendation 25).
Worsening on HFNC or NIV: do not delay intubation (ERS 2022, Results; BTS/ICS 2016, Recommendation 27).
precipitants: Heart failure (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 6.0).
Pulmonary embolism (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 6.0).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: pH below 7.35 and carbon dioxide above 6.5 kPa; target saturation 88% to 92% (BTS/ICS 2016, Definition and Recommendations 4 and 25).

differentials.condition: Carbon monoxide poisoning or acute blood loss
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abnormal quantity or type of haemoglobin rather than lung failure (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 6.0).

differentials.condition: Paraquat poisoning, acid inhalation or bleomycin lung injury
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Give oxygen with caution (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 7.0).

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Report at once; adjust oxygen to the prescribed target; monitor for at least 5 minutes after every change (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Sections 3.4 and 13.0).
ruleIn.normalValue: 96% to 98% awake at rest under 70 years; above 94% at 70 years and older (sea level)

clinicalManagement.title: Give oxygen to a target
actions: Critically ill or peri-arrest: 15 L/min via reservoir mask while awaiting review, including patients with COPD until blood gases are known (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.5).
Prescribe a target range for every patient: 94% to 98%, or 88% to 92% if at risk of hypercapnic failure (BTS 2017, Web Appendix 3).

clinicalManagement.title: Get a blood gas and find the cause
actions: Measure arterial blood gases; repeat after any sudden fall in saturation (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.4).
Get a chest X-ray and treat reversible causes (BTS/ICS 2016, Section Starting NIV in COPD).

clinicalManagement.title: Choose respiratory support
clinicalManagement.timeframe: If target not reached on conventional oxygen
actions: Hypoxaemic failure: use HFNC rather than conventional oxygen (ERS 2022, Recommendation PICO 1; conditional, moderate certainty).
Hypoxaemic failure: use HFNC rather than NIV (ERS 2022, Recommendation PICO 2; conditional, very low certainty).
Hypercapnic failure with pH below 7.35 and carbon dioxide above 6.5 kPa despite medical therapy: start NIV with target saturation 88% to 92% (BTS/ICS 2016, Recommendations 4 and 25).
COPD with hypercapnic failure: trial NIV before HFNC (ERS 2022, Recommendation on hypercapnic respiratory failure).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer to ICU early
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as support is escalated
actions: Monitor patients on HFNC or NIV closely with a team able to intubate promptly (ERS 2022, Results: PICO 2).
Do not let NIV delay escalation to IMV when IMV is more appropriate (BTS/ICS 2016, Recommendation 27).
Agree a ceiling of treatment and escalation plan at the start (BTS/ICS 2016, Recommendation 77).

clinicalManagement.title: Wean oxygen
actions: Step down oxygen when saturation stays above target and stop it in stable patients; keep the target range prescribed so oxygen can restart (BTS 2017, Web Appendix 3; NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 13.0).

regimens.patientGroup: Acutely ill adults without hypercapnia risk
regimens.dose: Titrate to saturation 94% to 98% (BTS 2017, Web Appendix 3); 15 L/min via reservoir mask if critically ill or peri-arrest (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.5).
regimens.route: Inhaled via nasal cannula, face mask, reservoir mask or HFNC
regimens.duration: Until saturation stays in the target range off oxygen
adjustments: Use the lowest fraction of inspired oxygen that meets the target (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 7.0).
Step down when saturation is above 98% for a sustained period (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 13.0).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Saturation for at least 5 minutes after each change (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 13.0).
Continuous oximetry if critically ill; record device and flow with each reading (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.4).
contraindications: No absolute contraindication when indicated; caution in paraquat poisoning, acid inhalation and previous bleomycin lung injury (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 7.0).
Fire hazard; drying of mucosa; absorption atelectasis (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 8.2).

regimens.indication: Acute hypoxaemia with risk of carbon dioxide retention
regimens.patientGroup: Adults at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure
regimens.dose: Titrate to saturation 88% to 92% (BTS 2017, Web Appendix 3); if critically ill, start at the same targets as other critically ill patients until blood gases are known (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.5).
regimens.route: Inhaled via controlled device; entrain close to the patient on NIV (BTS/ICS 2016, Recommendation 5)
regimens.duration: Until stable in the target range
adjustments: Drive nebulisers with compressed air and give oxygen by nasal prongs at 1 to 4 L/min alongside (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 11.0).
On NIV, optimise ventilator settings before raising inspired oxygen (BTS/ICS 2016, Recommendation 4 good practice point).

monitoring: Arterial blood gas before and after any change in support (BTS/ICS 2016, Section Starting NIV in COPD).
Saturation and respiratory rate (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.4).
contraindications: Excess oxygen raises carbon dioxide and worsens acidosis in this group (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 8.1).

medicationPlan.note: Oxygen is prescribed to a target saturation range rather than a fixed dose (BTS 2017, Web Appendix 3). HFNC flow, NIV pressures and ventilator settings are set by the treating team and are not listed. diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Target saturation, most acutely ill adults
Target saturation, at risk of hypercapnic failure

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: pH below 7.35 and carbon dioxide above 6.5 kPa; pH below 7.25 has been used as a threshold for considering IMV (BTS/ICS 2016, Definition of acute hypercapnic respiratory failure).
Arterial oxygen to inspired oxygen ratio (PaO2/FiO2) 200 mmHg or less, where HFNC and NIV are used more often (ERS 2022, Results: PICO 2 background).

teaching.scope: Adults with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure in the emergency department (ED) or on a ward: target-based oxygen prescribing, choice between conventional oxygen, high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) and non-invasive ventilation (NIV), recognition of hypercapnia, and timely referral to the intensive care unit (ICU) for invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV). Uses the British Thoracic Society (BTS) 2017 oxygen guideline summary, an NHS Borders policy adapted from the BTS guideline, the European Respiratory Society (ERS) 2022 high-flow guideline and the BTS/Intensive Care Society 2016 hypercapnic respiratory failure guideline. Disease-specific treatment (pneumonia, heart failure, pulmonary embolism) is in separate topics.
learningObjectives: Prescribe oxygen to a target saturation range.
Separate hypoxaemic from hypercapnic failure with a blood gas.
Prefer HFNC to NIV in hypoxaemic failure.
Refer to ICU before support fails.
pitfalls: Giving uncontrolled oxygen to a known carbon dioxide retainer after blood gases show hypercapnia.
Persisting with HFNC or NIV in a deteriorating patient.
Stepping up oxygen without checking the equipment.
keyPoints: 94% to 98% for most; 88% to 92% if at risk of hypercapnia.
Critically ill: 15 L/min reservoir mask first.
NIV is for hypercapnic acidosis; it should not delay intubation.

patientEducation: Oxygen is a medicine given to keep your blood oxygen in a safe range.
Tell staff if breathing gets harder or you feel drowsy or confused.
If you retain carbon dioxide, carry an oxygen alert card.
lifestyleAndDiet: No smoking or open flames near oxygen (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 8.2).
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; respiratory physician; critical care outreach and ICU team; physiotherapist; nursing staff for oxygen titration (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 3.3).
dischargeCriteria: Saturation in target range on air or on an assessed home-oxygen plan; cause treated; blood gases stable if hypercapnic; ceiling-of-care discussion recorded.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Follow-up with the respiratory or relevant specialty team for the underlying cause; long-term oxygen assessment only through the dedicated pathway (NHS Borders oxygen policy 2013, Section 4.0).
